note: Hand-declared, and checked against the leaves. What a form means is a judgement and no script has it, so every entry here is written by a person. What no person is trusted with is whether the form is actually in the books: each entry declares a pattern, `npm run glossary` searches the transcribed leaves for it, and an entry that matches nothing fails the build. The search runs over the books' own writing — the ruled rows, the headings the leaf carries, the work titles, the hands and the margins — and never over a `\note{}`, because the notes are where we discuss these forms and an entry could otherwise cite as evidence the sentence written because of it. The four notebooks are searched with the ledgers, and from 2026 the black notebook adds its own forms — her « c̄ » for with, her « ± » for about, the tick on a mailing list, the ordinal that looks like an inch mark.
means: Two columns, and the division is the whole point. « As written » is the leaf's, exactly, and is not a claim of ours. « Means » is ours, it is an expansion the transcription deliberately does not make, and it may be wrong. Nothing in the transcription is expanded — `Inv.` stays `Inv.` and `30 - 1/3` stays as written — because expanding would be normalisation, which is the one thing this edition refuses. This page is the key, kept outside the text it unlocks. In the lines quoted as evidence, │ marks a ruled column division on the leaf: what falls between two of them stood in one cell of the book's own ruling.

entries.means: Invited. The work was asked for by the exhibition, rather than submitted to its jury — which is why it stands where `A` and `R` otherwise stand, and why no verdict follows it.
Accepted · Refused. The jury's verdict, one letter in its own narrow column beside the date. A refusal is recorded as carefully as an acceptance, which is the most useful habit in Book I.
entries.note: The column is unheaded on most leaves and headed « accepted Refused » on leaf 8.

entries.means: Exhibition. Almost always followed by the society or the gallery that held it.
Society — the printmakers' and etchers' societies whose annuals Book I follows year by year.
The National Academy of Design, New York. It recurs on nearly every etching leaf, and it is the body that refused him most often.
Brooklyn — most often the Brooklyn Society of Etchers, whose annual he showed in from 1921, and the Brooklyn Museum that bought from it.
Commission — the dealer's share, and the thing that turns a price into a receipt. See `30 - 1/3` below.
Received. In Book I it heads the column of what actually came in; in Book IV it opens the red line under a charge — « rec'd by check » — that says the account is settled.
Reproduced. The work was printed somewhere — a magazine, a catalogue, a review — and she recorded it as carefully as a sale.
Gallery. « Rehn Gal. », « Downtown Gal. », « Babcock Gal. » — the same dealers she elsewhere writes out in full.
Museum.
Institute — the Art Institute of Chicago and the Carnegie Institute, chiefly.
American.
Water colour. One of the three medium markers that enter Book IV at leaf 109, written beside the title rather than in a column of their own.
Oil. The bare letter after a title, in the same position `w.c` and `E` take.
entries.note: The commonest one-letter marker and the easiest to misread as part of a title. It is a marker only where it stands after the title with nothing else on the line.

entries.means: Etching. The last of the three medium markers to appear, on Book IV leaf 119 in 1945.
Edward Hopper · Josephine Hopper — herself. She initials her own hand as readily as his.

A price and the dealer's share of it, and NOT a subtraction. « 30 - 1/3 » is a work priced at thirty dollars with a third to the dealer, leaving twenty. The fraction is the commission rate, written as a fraction or as a percentage indifferently, and the figure that follows in the next column is what the cheque actually came to.
entries.note: This is the single most misreadable form in the books. Read as arithmetic it turns a thirty-dollar etching into a work priced at twenty-nine and two-thirds.

entries.means: A sum in dollars and a vulgar fraction of one, which is what a third of a price comes to before anybody rounds. On the leaf the fraction is raised over lowered figures; the transcription sets it on the line as `2/3`.

The same money written as a decimal, which is what the right-hand columns hold. Book IV writes the point three ways — after the dollars, across the ruled division between the columns, or not at all — and all three are hers.

A ditto: this line repeats the line above, in that column. A row of nothing but dittoes is the row above it over again — a second cheque to the same client, most often — and it carries no new fact except its own figure.

The dollar sign, which she writes above and to the left of the figure and often detached from it. It is easy to attach to the wrong column when reading, and it reaches Book IV's money column only in the 1940s and only on the largest sums.

entries.standard: Frederick Keppel & Co., the print dealers
entries.means: Frederick Keppel & Co. She spells it « Keppel » four lines from where she spells it « Kepple », and both stand as written. Search for either.

The San Francisco print dealers, with the k gone from the first name and an r from the last. The Dealers volume spells the same firm « Vickery, Atkins & Tory », so all three forms are in the corpus and none of them is the firm's own.

entries.standard: Frank Crowninshield, editor of Vanity Fair
entries.means: Frank Crowninshield, spelt three ways across Book I — « Crowninshield » on leaves 6 and 10, this on leaf 12. All stay.
Grace Horne's, without the e. Boston, and a gallery rather than the tea room the name suggests.

entries.standard: John Clancy, of the Rehn Gallery
entries.means: John Clancy, who ran the Rehn Gallery after Rehn's death. Book IV writes « Clancy » and « Clancey » on facing leaves, and Book I spells it with the e on leaf 67.

entries.standard: Osgood, on the usual spelling of the name — but nothing in these books establishes it.
entries.means: The single largest buyer of the 1924 and 1925 watercolours. She writes « Osgord » on leaves 59, 60, 61, 62, 63 and 66 and never once « Osgood »: six leaves and one spelling is not a slip of the pen, so this entry records what the books have and points at where, rather than correcting her to the name a reader would expect.
With an e, on leaves 56, 57, 79 and 92 and in three work titles. The catalogue clipping pasted to leaf 56 prints « Cape Anne, Massachusetts » too, so the spelling is not only hers.
One g, on leaves 62, 64, 66 and 86. She writes « Fogg » correctly elsewhere in the same book, which is why both forms have to be searched for and neither can be normalised away.
With — a small c under a macron, the prescription's abbreviation: « c̄ B. Hartman » heads the frame recipe, « Truro, trip c̄ Manchester » opens 1959. The black notebook's; the ledgers never use it.
Bought — « Bgt. by » before a buyer's name throughout Book I's etching leaves, and in the black notebook « bgt. Ap. 4, 1960 » for the phonograph and « Bgt. land. » under 1933 for the Truro plot.
Hospital — New York Hospital, in the black notebook's chronicle of operations from 1948, where « 3" trip N.Y. Hos. » is a third stay; the ledgers' Book I has it too.

Washington Square — 3 Washington Square North, the studio. The ledgers' « Painted in Wash. Sq. studio », the notebooks' lists of who lived and visited there, and the Square itself in the campaign of 1947.
The Metropolitan Museum of Art, throughout: its purchases in the ledgers, and in the notebook the jury she flew to New York for in 1952 and its water colour show.

About. A plus over a bar after a date, a figure or a size she was not sure of: Book III's sizes carry it, Book I gives it once for a Paris watercolour, and the black notebook dates by it — « Ap. 17 ±, 1953 », « 1954 ± ».

A tick against a name on a mailing list. Her two keys disagree, one leaf apart: page 52 of the black notebook says « √ = came or wrote », page 53 « √ = wrote or rec'd. by hand) √√ came ». Both are hers, and neither governs the other page.

An ordinal, not an inch mark: the raised double stroke after a day of the month or a count is her « th », in the ledgers' receipt dates as in the notebook's — Dec. 6th, the third trip. The same stroke after a dimension is inches, and alone in a column it is a ditto; which it is depends on what stands before it.

entries.standard: Saltillo, Coahuila — which she also spells correctly, once on the same page as « Sattillo »
entries.means: Three times « Sattillo » and three « Sortillo » across the black notebook's chronicles and its list of the Mexican journeys, against « Saltillo » on page 44 and in the ledgers' titles.

entries.standard: Whatman, the water colour paper, by the half sheet
entries.means: On the water colour sizes of pages 6 and 40: « Watman" 1/2 sheet - 15 x 22 », « 1/2 sheet Watmans = 22 1/2 x 15 1/2 ».

entries.standard: The Wadsworth Atheneum, Hartford — two spellings on one leaf, neither the museum's
entries.means: On the museum staff list of page 31, where the Wadsworth is written both ways within six lines, and again on page 35.
Under 1938 in the year chronicle, « Cape Huricane », and once more.

entries.standard: Cooper Union, where she priced water colour paper by the pound
entries.means: On page 8, pricing 72 lb and 140 lb paper against Robinson's.
